about: Exercises with the PhET Band Structure simulation (Many Wells). Answers computed with the simulation's own solver: notes/solid-state/build/phet/README.md.

enc.title: PhET: from one well to a band

sim.name: PhET Band Structure
sim.setup: Open the Many Wells (Band Structure) tab. Square wells, width 0.5 nm, height 10 eV, separation 0.1 nm, offset 0, particle mass 1.0 (the defaults: "Configure Potential..." shows them; "Reset" restores them). Set Number of Wells to 1 first. Read energies off the energy axis; the magnifying glass helps with close levels, clicking a level shows its wave function.
sim.credit: PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder (CC-BY).

enc.problem: A crystal is many atoms side by side. In the sim each atom is a square potential well; electrons tunnel through the barriers between them. Start with a single well, then add wells and watch what happens to each energy level.

steps.prompt: One well: how many bound levels lie below the barrier top (10 eV)?
steps.hint: Count the horizontal lines inside the well. Estimate: $z_0=\frac{w}{2}\sqrt{2mV_0}/\hbar=0.25\,\mathrm{nm}\times\sqrt{10\,\mathrm{eV}/0.0381\,\mathrm{eV\,nm^2}}=4.05$, and a finite well has $\lceil 2z_0/\pi\rceil=3$ bound states.

steps.prompt: One well: energy of the ground state (eV).
steps.hint: The infinite well would give $\pi^2\hbar^2/2mw^2=1.50$ eV; the finite well is lower because the wave function leaks into the barriers ($z\tan z=\sqrt{z_0^2-z^2}$ gives $z=1.257$, $E=0.963$ eV). The sim shows 0.967 eV.

steps.prompt: Now set 5 wells. What happens to the single-well ground level near 0.97 eV?
options: It stays one level at 0.97 eV, only the wave function spreads
It splits into 5 closely spaced levels around 0.97 eV: a band
It splits into 10 levels (two spins per well)
It moves up because the wells repel each other

why.0: Tunnelling couples the wells: the $N$ degenerate single-well states mix into $N$ different combinations with different energies.
why.2: The sim has no spin: each spatial state would hold 2 electrons, but there are $N$ spatial levels, not $2N$.
why.3: The levels spread both down and up around the single-well energy (bonding-like combinations go down).

steps.after: Each single-well level becomes a band of $N$ levels: here 0.81, 0.86, 0.95, 1.02, 1.08 eV.

steps.prompt: 5 wells: width of the lowest band, top level minus bottom level (eV).
steps.hint: Read the lowest (0.81 eV) and the highest (1.08 eV) of the 5 lowest lines: the band is 0.27 eV wide.

steps.prompt: Set 10 wells: how many levels does the second band have?
steps.hint: Every band has exactly $N$ levels for $N$ wells (one per atom). With spin each holds 2 electrons, so a band holds $2N$ electrons.

source.where: PhET Band Structure 1.08 (Many Wells), energies from the sim's own solver, see notes/solid-state/build/phet/README.md

enc.title: PhET: tight binding predicts the band width

sim.name: PhET Band Structure
sim.setup: Square wells, width 0.5 nm, height 10 eV, separation 0.1 nm, offset 0, particle mass 1.0 (the defaults: "Configure Potential..." shows them; "Reset" restores them). Use the Many Wells tab and change only the number of wells.
sim.credit: PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder (CC-BY).

enc.problem: Script 3.2 (tight binding): one orbital per site with nearest-neighbour hopping $B$. For an infinite chain $E(k)=E_i-A_i-2B\cos ka$, so the band is $4B$ wide. For a finite chain of $N$ sites (as in the sim, hard walls at the ends) the levels are $E_j=E_0-2B\cos\frac{j\pi}{N+1}$, $j=1\ldots N$. Measure $B$ with two wells and predict the rest.

steps.prompt: 2 wells: the ground level splits into a pair. Half of the splitting is $B$. Value of $B$ (eV)?
steps.hint: With $N=2$: $E_{1,2}=E_0\mp2B\cos\frac\pi3=E_0\mp B$, so the splitting is $2B$. Levels 0.885 and 1.033 eV: $B=0.074$ eV.

steps.prompt: Prediction for 5 wells: band width $E_5-E_1=4B\cos\frac{\pi}{6}$ (eV). Then check it in the sim.
steps.hint: $4\times0.074\times0.866=0.255$ eV; the sim shows 0.272 eV (the simple model ignores next-nearest neighbours and overlap): within 7 %.

steps.prompt: Width of the band for a very long chain, $4B$ (eV). Compare with 10 wells in the sim.
steps.hint: $4B=0.295$ eV; with 10 wells the sim already gives $1.0997-0.8056=0.294$ eV: the band fills its final width quickly.

steps.prompt: Effective mass at the band bottom, $m^*/m_e=\dfrac{\hbar^2/2m_e}{Ba^2}$ with the period $a=w+s=0.6$ nm and $\hbar^2/2m_e=0.0381$ eV nm$^2$.
steps.hint: From $E\approx E_0-2B+Bk^2a^2$: $\frac{\hbar^2}{2m^*}=Ba^2$. $0.0381/(0.074\times0.36)=1.4$: a narrow band means heavy electrons.

steps.prompt: Click the lowest and the highest level of the band (5 wells). How do the wave functions look between the wells?
options: Lowest: the same sign in every well (no node between wells); highest: the sign alternates from well to well
Lowest: alternating signs; highest: all the same sign
Both look the same, only the amplitude differs
Lowest is in the middle well only, highest in the outer wells

why.1: Alternating signs put a node in every barrier: that costs kinetic energy, so it is the top of the band ($ka=\pi$).
why.2: They differ in the relative phase between wells, which is exactly what sets the energy.
why.3: All band states spread over all wells (Bloch-like), with an envelope $\sin\frac{j\pi n}{N+1}$.

steps.after: Bottom of the band = all in phase ($k=0$, bonding); top = alternating ($k=\pi/a$, antibonding). Same pattern as the two-well molecule (Bonding Grotto).

source.where: PhET Band Structure 1.08 (Many Wells), energies from the sim's own solver, see notes/solid-state/build/phet/README.md

enc.title: PhET: barrier width and tunnelling

sim.name: PhET Band Structure
sim.setup: Many Wells tab, 5 wells, width 0.5 nm, height 10 eV, mass 1.0. Change only the separation in "Configure Potential..." (0.05 to 0.2 nm).
sim.credit: PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder (CC-BY).

enc.problem: The hopping $B$ comes from tunnelling through the barrier, so it should fall like $e^{-\kappa s}$ with the barrier width $s$ and $\kappa=\sqrt{2m(V-E)}/\hbar$ (as in the QM tunnelling bridge).

steps.prompt: Lowest band width at separation 0.2 nm (eV).
steps.hint: Bottom 0.939 eV, top 0.994 eV: 0.056 eV, five times narrower than at 0.1 nm (0.272 eV).

steps.prompt: Ratio of the lowest band widths, separation 0.15 nm divided by 0.10 nm.
steps.hint: 0.124 eV / 0.272 eV = 0.46. Every extra 0.05 nm of barrier multiplies the width by about the same factor: exponential dependence.

steps.prompt: Decay constant in the barrier for the lowest band, $\kappa=\sqrt{(V-E)/(\hbar^2/2m)}$ with $V-E\approx10-0.97$ eV (nm$^{-1}$).
steps.hint: $\sqrt{9.03/0.0381}=15.4$ nm$^{-1}$: the wave function drops by $e$ every 0.065 nm inside the barrier.

steps.prompt: Tunnelling prediction for the ratio, $e^{-\kappa\,\Delta s}$ with $\Delta s=0.05$ nm. Compare with your measurement.
steps.hint: $e^{-15.4\times0.05}=0.46$, the measured ratio: the band width is a tunnelling amplitude.

steps.prompt: At separation 0.1 to 0.15 nm the second band shrinks only by a factor 0.52, the first by 0.46. Why?
options: The second band lies closer to the barrier top, so $\kappa$ is smaller and the tunnelling decays more slowly with $s$
The second band has more levels
The second band feels a lower barrier because of the offset
Higher bands are not formed by tunnelling but by reflection

why.2: The offset shifts all energies equally; it does not change $V-E$.
why.3: All bound bands come from coupling through the barriers; higher ones simply couple more strongly.

steps.after: $V-E\approx6.2$ eV gives $\kappa=12.8$ nm$^{-1}$ and $e^{-0.64}=0.53$. Higher, less bound states overlap more: higher bands are wider (0.27, 1.09, 2.38 eV here).

source.where: PhET Band Structure 1.08 (Many Wells), energies from the sim's own solver, see notes/solid-state/build/phet/README.md

enc.title: PhET: lighter particles, deeper wells

sim.name: PhET Band Structure
sim.setup: Many Wells tab, 5 wells, width 0.5 nm, separation 0.1 nm. Change the particle mass slider, then the height.
sim.credit: PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder (CC-BY).

enc.problem: The same tunnelling picture predicts how the band width depends on the particle mass and the barrier height. Check the predictions.

steps.prompt: Predict first: what happens to the lowest band when the mass is lowered from 1.0 to 0.5 $m_e$?
options: It moves up and becomes much wider
It moves up and becomes narrower
Nothing: band widths depend only on the geometry
It moves down and becomes wider

why.1: Smaller $m$ means smaller $\kappa\propto\sqrt m$: more tunnelling, a wider band.
why.2: The mass enters both the kinetic energy and $\kappa$.
why.3: Confinement energies scale as $1/m$: the levels go up.

steps.after: Lighter: confinement energy up ($\propto1/m$) and $\kappa\propto\sqrt{m(V-E)}$ down, so much stronger coupling.

steps.prompt: Lowest band width at mass 0.5 $m_e$ (eV).
steps.hint: 1.15 to 2.06 eV: 0.92 eV, more than three times the 0.27 eV at $m_e$.

steps.prompt: Back to mass 1.0. Lowest band width at height 20 eV (eV).
steps.hint: 1.020 to 1.142 eV: 0.12 eV. A higher barrier means larger $\kappa$ and less overlap: tighter binding, narrower band (and a heavier $m^*$).

steps.prompt: Which real materials does "heavy particle, high barrier" describe?
options: Inner atomic shells and d/f electrons: narrow bands, heavy carriers
Free-electron metals like Na
Semiconductors with light electrons
Insulators only

why.1: Na has a wide, nearly free-electron band (weak periodic potential).
why.2: Light carriers come from wide bands with strong overlap.
why.3: Narrow bands occur in metals too (transition metals, heavy fermions).

steps.after: Tightly bound orbitals overlap little: narrow bands. The tight-binding limit of the script; the nearly-free-electron limit is the opposite end (wide bands, small gaps $2|U_G|$).

source.where: PhET Band Structure 1.08 (Many Wells), energies from the sim's own solver, see notes/solid-state/build/phet/README.md

enc.title: PhET: metal or insulator by counting electrons

sim.name: PhET Band Structure
sim.setup: Many Wells tab, 10 wells, otherwise the defaults (width 0.5 nm, height 10 eV, separation 0.1 nm, mass 1.0).
sim.credit: PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder (CC-BY).

enc.problem: Each band of an $N$-atom chain has $N$ levels and holds $2N$ electrons (spin). Fill the levels from the bottom and look at the gap between the highest occupied and the lowest empty level.

steps.prompt: Two electrons per well (20 electrons): energy gap between the highest filled and the lowest empty level (eV).
steps.hint: 20 electrons fill all 10 levels of band 1 (top 1.100 eV); the next level is the bottom of band 2 (3.193 eV): a 2.09 eV gap. An insulator (or semiconductor).

steps.prompt: One electron per well (10 electrons): gap between the highest filled and the lowest empty level (eV).
steps.hint: 10 electrons fill the lowest 5 levels; level 5 is 0.917 eV, level 6 is 0.960 eV: only 0.044 eV, and it shrinks like $1/N$. For a real crystal ($N\sim10^{23}$) it vanishes: a metal.

steps.prompt: Compare with $k_BT=0.026$ eV at room temperature. Which statement is right?
options: Half-filled band: excitations cost nothing in a large crystal, so it conducts; full band: $2$ eV $\gg k_BT$, so it does not
Both conduct because $k_BT$ is not zero
Both insulate because there are always gaps between levels
The full band conducts better because it has more electrons

why.1: Thermal excitation across 2 eV is suppressed by $e^{-2/0.026}\sim10^{-34}$.
why.2: In a macroscopic crystal the level spacing inside a band is $\sim$ bandwidth/$N$, effectively zero.
why.3: A full band carries no net current: for every $k$ there is a $-k$.

steps.after: Odd number of electrons per cell in 1D: metal. Even: insulator, unless bands overlap (possible in 3D, e.g. Mg, Zn), as in the nearly-free-electron lab.

source.where: PhET Band Structure 1.08 (Many Wells), energies from the sim's own solver, see notes/solid-state/build/phet/README.md
